claims.text: None of the retrieved material reports a measured frequency of large functions failing to match due to inlining choices, per project or per compiler version. The sources give project lists, completion percentages and general statements that CodeWarrior's optimization decisions are hard to predict, but no failure-rate data. Any estimate for effort on large functions would have to come from sampling a project directly.

claims.text: The Wii decomp tracker lists projects at very different maturity: Petari (Super Mario Galaxy) and Mario Strikers Charged are complete at 100%, while Wii Sports is at 35.03%, Xenoblade at 10.77% and Brawl at 1.73%. Completed or high-progress projects are the ones where hard, inlining-sensitive large functions have already been resolved or left as known blockers, so they are the best candidates for mining commit history and issue trackers for measurements. The compiler range cited is CodeWarrior 1.0 through 1.7 across titles, but no per-project version mapping is given.

This means a per-project inlining-failure count would have to be assembled from these outputs, not read from documentation.

claims.text: Inlining copies a helper's body into every call site, so the large caller no longer contains a call at all. Optimization then runs on the enlarged body, with constants propagated, branches eliminated and registers allocated across the combined code. The instruction order and register choices in the large function therefore depend on whether the helper was inlined, and they differ from the not-inlined case, where arguments are passed and a call is made.

meta.query: Why does the compiler produce different code for a large function when a small helper is inlined, not inlined, or emitted as a separate deduplicated copy, and how does that change the instruction order and register choices a decompiler has to reproduce?
meta.capability: You can stop assuming a decompiler or reverse-engineering effort will see the same function structure the source author wrote, and budget for the fact that the compiler merges, duplicates, or discards helper functions depending on build settings.

claims.text: The same helper can end up inlined at some call sites while an out-of-line copy still exists, for example when its address is taken or the compiler judges it too large. In C++, an unexpanded helper is emitted as a shared copy that the linker merges across translation units. In C, a static helper instead gets a separate copy per translation unit. So the deduplicated-copy case is a linkage outcome, not just an optimizer choice.

meta.query: Why does the compiler produce different code for a large function when a small helper is inlined, not inlined, or emitted as a separate deduplicated copy, and how does that change the instruction order and register choices a decompiler has to reproduce?
meta.capability: You can predict which helpers will have survived as separate callable code in a binary, and stop expecting a single outcome (inlined, not inlined, or one shared copy) for a given helper.

claims.text: Inline markings do not force inlining. Debug builds with MSVC's default setting disable it entirely, and even forced inlining is refused for recursion, varargs, or mismatched exception handling. Rust never inlines in debug mode. The same source therefore compiles to structurally different code per build mode, and the original build flags matter as much as the source.

meta.query: Why does the compiler produce different code for a large function when a small helper is inlined, not inlined, or emitted as a separate deduplicated copy, and how does that change the instruction order and register choices a decompiler has to reproduce?
meta.capability: You can treat the build configuration, such as debug versus optimized builds, as a first-order input when assessing whether recovered code can match the original, instead of assuming the source's inline markings decide the outcome.

claims.text: Heavier inlining makes the compiled program larger, which can cause more instruction-cache misses and slow the program down in workloads under cache pressure. So the most aggressive optimization level is not always the fastest, and the claim has to be checked by profiling both builds.

meta.query: At what function size or complexity do attempts to reproduce the original compiled bytes stop converging, and what do the stuck attempts look like when the cause is inlining rather than constructors, destructors or exception handling?
meta.capability: You can stop assuming that more aggressive compiler optimization is automatically better for your software's speed, and ask engineering to measure both settings before committing.

claims.text: The retrieved material is about C++ language mechanics, not matching-decompilation practice, so it cannot say how people prove a difference is unreachable. It does show that compilers insert copy-constructor calls, and extra moves from pass-by-value parameters, that the author never wrote. Output differences can therefore come from compiler-generated behavior that no rewrite of the visible source controls, which suggests setting a stopping rule for repeated rewrites.

meta.query: What happens when a large function with templates, member-pointer calls, copy constructors, or deeply nested inline calls is rewritten many times and still does not match, and how do people tell that the remaining difference is unreachable from source code?
meta.capability: You can stop assuming that every remaining difference in compiled output is a flaw in the source code, and cap the engineering time spent on rewrites that keep failing to match.

claims.text: Snowboard Kids 2 stalled twice after the first AI-driven jumps (about 25% to 58%, then to about 75%), yet reached 100% on May 17, 2026, 596 days after the first commit. The last 10 especially hard functions were largely closed by community members, and the maintainer says the community mattered more than any model. Stalls reflect the ordering strategy (easiest first, give up after 10 failed attempts) rather than true impossibility.

meta.query: Which functions in matching-decompilation projects were declared impossible to match and later turned out to match after all, and what did the people who finally matched them change that the earlier attempts missed?
meta.capability: You can stop accepting 'this function is impossible to match' as a final verdict and instead treat stalled work as a sign that the easy-first method has run out, not that the code can't be done.

claims.text: On Snowboard Kids, about 4.8% of matching commits (roughly 41) involved experts familiar with SGI's IDO compiler. The maintainer estimates that without them the match rate might have plateaued at around 89-90%. The estimate is the maintainer's own and is not a measured value.

claims.text: Register assignment and spilling are decided by the compiler backend from live-range overlap, spill weights and the target's calling rules, so hand-reusing variables or restructuring code does not help and can hurt. Spilled values are what enlarge the stack frame, so frame size is an allocator outcome, not a source property. The advice is to profile first and trust the allocator unless hot-loop spilling is shown.
claims.ledger_reason: no quote verified in any snapshot

rejected_quotes.quote: Manually “optimizing” C code by reusing variables (e.g., temp = a; ... temp = b;) does not help — it actually hurts.

Spilled registers are precisely the reason those stack frames expand — every spill slot adds 8 bytes (on a 64-bit architecture) to the frame size, which the prologue must reserve via sub rsp, N or sub

meta.query: Why does the same source code produce different register assignments, stack frame sizes and instruction ordering when a compiler is built or run slightly differently, and which of these differences can source rewriting never fix?
meta.capability: You can stop spending engineering time rewriting source code to shrink stack frames or change register use, and instead direct that effort to profiling and to compiler settings and target choice.

claims.text: The same source yields different register and stack outcomes across platforms because the calling convention and register file are fixed by the target, not the code. In the one worked example, a function with 8 parameters had its last two passed on the stack on x86-64 System V (first 6 in registers), whereas ARM64 passed all 8 in registers with no stack access. Windows x64 differs again, passing 4 in registers and requiring 32 bytes of caller-allocated shadow space, so no rewrite can equalise these.

meta.query: Why does the same source code produce different register assignments, stack frame sizes and instruction ordering when a compiler is built or run slightly differently, and which of these differences can source rewriting never fix?
meta.capability: You can expect different binaries, frame sizes and register use when you change target CPU, operating system or compiler vendor, and budget for that instead of treating it as a bug in your code.

claims.text: Compilers and CPUs reorder independent instructions freely, and the result varies with context, hardware and surrounding code. Only data dependencies are preserved, which is safe for single-threaded programs but can break multithreaded code that lacks locks, atomics or barriers. Vendors also implement named conventions like fastcall differently, so mixing compilers can break interoperability.

meta.query: Why does the same source code produce different register assignments, stack frame sizes and instruction ordering when a compiler is built or run slightly differently, and which of these differences can source rewriting never fix?
meta.capability: You can stop expecting two compiler builds to agree on instruction order or on 'fastcall'-style conventions, and plan to verify behaviour, such as concurrency correctness, rather than machine-code equality.

claims.text: Reported match figures use different units: decomp.dev's code match rate counts matched code bytes, Heumann's 83% for Modern Warfare 2 counts matched functions out of all functions, and his 99% counts functions with any reconstructed source. A Halo fork's README claims 99.5% byte matching while the original repository on decomp.dev shows 23.25% (2,511 of 11,047 functions), with no definition given for the README figure, so a headline number can mean something very different from what it appears to.

claims.text: The linker can merge functions whose generated machine code is byte-identical, so one piece of code ends up with two names and a debugger arbitrarily shows the wrong one. Whether two different functions end up identical depends on the compiler version and optimization settings, and is very frequent with templates, so the same pattern can be merged in one build and not in another.

meta.capability: You can stop trusting that two functions identical in source or behavior will stay distinct in the shipped program, and expect the debugging and analysis tools to report one for the other.

claims.text: Because merging happens at link time and depends on the build, a developer or support team can be sent to a function that was never actually called, with no change in the source. This is a tooling artifact that can be switched off with a linker setting, so it should be ruled out before spending engineering time chasing a phantom bug.

claims.text: Compilers apply only low-level, semantics-preserving transformations, and each one is conditional on context. For example, a repeated array read is reused only if no write to the array can occur on any path in between, so the same expression is optimized in one block and left alone in another. Optimizations also chain, so one pass exposes or removes work for the next, which makes the outcome sensitive to what surrounds the code.

claims.text: AI coding agents have compressed decompile-and-rebuild work for new hardware from months to hours or days, and the technique has carried across very different targets: a 2003 PC RTS to iOS, Halo and GTA V into web browsers, PS4's Bloodborne to native PC, and even a Switch 2 jailbreak. The reported limit is that classic games have relatively low code complexity, so the compression is best demonstrated on older titles, not modern large codebases.
